questions.q: As verified in this lesson, which model is described as Anthropic's flagship reasoning tier, open to all customers, as of October 2026?
options: Claude Haiku 4.5
Claude Fable 5.1
Claude Sonnet 5.5
Claude 3 Opus
questions.explain: Claude Fable 5.1 is described directly in Anthropic's own documentation as its most capable model open to all customers, built for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work.

questions.q: What does the "family" part of a model name (like Claude, GPT, or Gemini) identify?
options: The exact release date of the model
The programming language the model was built with
The country where the model was trained
The lineage or brand, not a specific callable model by itself
questions.explain: A family name identifies the overall lineage (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, Llama); a specific callable model also needs a generation and tier.

questions.q: What makes Meta's Llama different from Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's GPT in terms of access, per this lesson?
options: Meta open-weights Llama rather than operating a hosted API the way Anthropic and OpenAI do
Llama is only available in one country
Llama cannot process any text input
Llama requires a paid government license to use
questions.explain: Meta releases Llama's weights for download rather than primarily operating a hosted API, which Lesson 9 covers as the open-weight vs. closed distinction.

questions.q: In a name like "Claude Sonnet 5.5," what does "Sonnet" indicate?
options: The exact release year
The programming framework used to build it
The tier — where this model sits on the speed-vs-capability trade-off within its family
The country of origin
questions.explain: The tier name (Sonnet, in this case) indicates where the model sits on the balance between speed, cost, and capability, as covered in Lesson 6.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend checking each provider's own documentation directly rather than relying on memorized model lists?
options: Because provider documentation is always wrong
Because model lineups change quickly enough that any static list, including this lesson's, will eventually be out of date
Because providers legally require it
Because memorized lists are always more accurate
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames its own list as a snapshot checked in October 2026, not a permanent fact to memorize, since the landscape changes quickly (the subject of Lesson 12).
